title: “SHOULD YOUR SPRINGS BE SCATTERED ABROAD?” THE SEXUAL METAPHOR HIDDEN IN PROVERBS 5
paragraphs: “SHOULD YOUR SPRINGS BE SCATTERED ABROAD?” THE SEXUAL METAPHOR HIDDEN IN PROVERBS 5
The Bible Says Something About Sexual Desire That Many Christians Were Never Taught—and It May Change the Way You Understand Temptation, Marriage, Shame, and Grace
There is a sentence in Proverbs that sounds almost innocent in English.
Until you understand what Solomon is talking about.
“Should your springs be dispersed outside, your streams of water in the wide plazas?” — Proverbs 5:16
Springs.
Water.
Streets.
At first glance, it sounds like irrigation.
It isn’t.
And when you read the words surrounding it, the meaning becomes impossible to ignore.

This is Scripture speaking with startling honesty about sexual desire, marital faithfulness, temptation, pleasure, consequences, and the devastating human tendency to pour something sacred into places where it was never meant to go.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 5:16 reads:
יָפוּצוּ מַעְיְנֹתֶיךָ חוּצָה בָּרְחֹבוֹת פַּלְגֵי־מָיִם
Yāfūtsū maʿyenōteykhā ḥūtsāh, bārəḥōvōt palgê-māyim.
Literally, the picture is of “your springs” being dispersed outside and streams of water flowing in the public squares.

The verb יָפוּצוּ, yāfūtsū, carries the idea of being scattered or dispersed. מַעְיְנֹתֶיךָ, maʿyenōteykhā, means “your springs” or “your fountains.” חוּצָה, ḥūtsāh, points outward—outside. Then comes בָּרְחֹבוֹת, bārəḥōvōt: in the broad places, streets, or public squares.
But Proverbs does not leave the metaphor floating without context.
The verse immediately before it says:
שְׁתֵה־מַיִם מִבּוֹרֶךָ וְנֹזְלִים מִתּוֹךְ בְּאֵרֶךָ
“Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.” — Proverbs 5:15
Then comes the question about scattering your springs abroad.
Then:
“Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.” — Proverbs 5:17
And then the imagery becomes unmistakably marital:

“May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife you married in your youth—a loving doe, a graceful deer; may her breasts satisfy you at all times, may you be captivated by her love always.” — Proverbs 5:18–19
The water is not really the point.
Faithfulness is.
Desire is.
Sexual intimacy is.
Covenant is.
And the question beneath the question is devastating:
Why would you take what belongs inside covenant and scatter it outside?

The NET Bible notes that the “springs” being dispersed form part of an extended metaphor contrasting exclusive marital intimacy with sexual activity outside marriage. Scholarly interpreters broadly recognize Proverbs 5:15–20 as erotic imagery urging marital faithfulness, although they differ over precisely how narrowly each water image should be identified. Some interpreters understand the springs and streams in verses 16–17 specifically as imagery for male sexual potency or semen; others treat the imagery more broadly as the husband’s sexuality and sexual expression. Either way, the central message does not depend upon choosing the narrowest interpretation: sexual desire is not condemned, but it is directed toward covenant faithfulness.
That distinction matters.
Because some Christians grew up believing that holiness meant pretending sexuality barely existed.
Don’t talk about it.
Don’t admit temptation.
Don’t admit desire.
Don’t ask questions.
And if you failed sexually, hide it quickly enough that nobody discovers what happened.
But Proverbs 5 does something radically different.
God does not whisper awkwardly about sexuality.
He speaks directly into it.
The same chapter that warns about adultery also tells a husband to delight in his wife.
The same chapter that warns against forbidden sexual pleasure celebrates covenant sexual pleasure.
That means the biblical message is not:
Desire is dirty.
The message is:
Desire is powerful.
And powerful things must be guarded.
Fire inside a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire unleashed through the house can destroy it.
Water directed into the right place gives life.
Water scattered where it does not belong is wasted.
And sexual desire—one of the strongest appetites many human beings will ever experience—is capable of bonding, delight, tenderness, vulnerability, procreation, companionship, and covenant intimacy.
But separated from faithfulness, that same appetite can leave wreckage behind.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that wreckage feels like.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been watching after everyone goes to sleep.
Maybe nobody knows about the messages you deleted.
The second account.
The private conversation.
The emotional attachment you keep calling “just friendship.”
The pornography history you clear.
The flirtation you justify because “nothing physical happened.”
The fantasy you keep feeding.
The person you know you should stop contacting.
The marriage you have emotionally abandoned while still sleeping in the same house.
Or maybe you are not the person who wandered.
Maybe you are the person who was wounded by somebody else’s wandering.
You discovered the messages.
You saw the browser history.
You heard the confession.
You found out there was another person.
And suddenly a sentence from Proverbs written thousands of years ago does not feel ancient at all.
“Should your springs be scattered abroad?”

That question reaches through history and sits beside us in the age of smartphones, disappearing messages, private browsing, dating apps, pornography, secret accounts, emotional affairs, and endless digital access to bodies that do not belong to us.
The technology changed.
The human heart did not.
We are still tempted to scatter what God calls us to steward.
And notice something uncomfortable about Proverbs 5.
The chapter does not merely say, “Adultery is against the rules.”
It shows where the road goes.
Earlier in the chapter, temptation is described as sweet at first and bitter afterward.
That is how sin often works.
Sin rarely introduces itself by showing you the funeral.
It shows you the kiss.
It does not show you the spouse crying in another room.
It shows you excitement.
It does not show you the child wondering why the family changed.
It shows you secrecy.
It does not show you the morning after exposure.
It shows you pleasure without showing you the invoice.
It whispers:
Nobody will know.
You deserve this.
Your marriage is complicated.
It is only online.
You can stop whenever you want.
You are lonely.
God understands.
Just this once.
And somewhere between “just this once” and “how did my life become this?” chains begin forming.
Proverbs 5:22 says that the wicked person can become caught in the cords of his own sin.
That is one of Scripture’s terrifying pictures of repeated sin.
At first you hold it.
Eventually it holds you.
But this is where the Gospel must enter the room.
Because if this article ends only with “control yourself,” we have not yet reached Christianity.
Christianity is not the announcement that good people behaved themselves while dirty people ruined their lives.
Christianity begins with the devastating truth that all of us need mercy.
Sexual sin is serious.
But sexual sin is not stronger than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Adultery is not stronger.
Pornography is not stronger.
Promiscuity is not stronger.
Lust is not stronger.
Your secret history is not stronger.
The night you wish you could erase is not stronger.
The relationship you should never have entered is not stronger.
Your shame is not stronger.
Jesus did not go to the cross because our sins were small.
He went because our need was enormous.
And the scandal of grace is that Christ does not merely expose sinners.
He saves sinners.
He does not call evil good. He does something infinitely better.
He forgives the guilty who come to Him.
The Gospel never says your sin did not matter.
The cross says it mattered so much that redemption required blood.
And then the empty tomb announces that sin and death did not get the final word.
This is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning house.
Jesus does not say, “Keep hiding until you become worthy enough to come home.”
He calls you to turn.
Confess.
Forsake what is destroying you.
Bring darkness into light.
Stop protecting the secret that is poisoning your soul.
If you are married and crossing boundaries with somebody else, stop calling compromise compassion.
If pornography owns a hidden room in your life, stop decorating the prison.
If you are feeding an emotional affair, stop waiting for physical adultery before calling it dangerous.
If your phone has become the doorway through which temptation repeatedly enters, radical obedience may feel inconvenient—but chains are more expensive.
Jesus spoke with frightening seriousness about lust in Matthew 5:27–30. His language makes clear that discipleship does not negotiate casually with what leads us into sin.
Not because God hates sexuality.
Proverbs 5 destroys that excuse.
God created sexuality.
The chapter can warn against illicit desire and then, without embarrassment, tell a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth and be continually captivated by her love.
Biblical holiness is not hatred of the body.
It is the surrender of the body to God.
And that changes the question.
The question is no longer merely:
“How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
The better question becomes:
“Jesus, what part of me have I still refused to surrender to You?”
My eyes?
My imagination?
My phone?
My loneliness?
My marriage?
My resentment?
My sexual history?
My appetite for attention?
My need to feel desired?
My secret life?
Because sometimes what looks like a sexual problem has roots far beneath sexuality.
Sometimes a person is trying to medicate rejection.
Sometimes loneliness.
Sometimes resentment.
Sometimes insecurity.
Sometimes trauma.
Sometimes boredom.
Sometimes the desperate need to feel wanted.
None of those things make sin righteous.
But understanding the wound can help expose why we keep reaching for the wrong medicine.
You can drink salt water for hours and still die of thirst.
That may be one of the deepest pictures hidden inside Proverbs 5.
You are thirsty.
But not every source of water will give you life.
Somebody else’s spouse cannot heal you.
Pornography cannot love you.
A stranger’s body cannot tell you who you are.
Being sexually desired cannot give you an identity secure enough to survive rejection.
An affair cannot repair the emptiness inside you.
Another secret encounter cannot silence your conscience permanently.
You were made for something deeper than endless appetite.
You were made for God.
And even marriage itself cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Your husband cannot be Jesus.
Your wife cannot be Jesus.
Sex cannot be Jesus.
Romance cannot be Jesus.
Only Christ can occupy the throne of the human heart without destroying the person who puts Him there.
That is why the Christian answer to sexual brokenness is ultimately not repression.
It is redemption.
Not “pretend you have no desires.”
But “bring your desires under the lordship of Christ.”
Not “you sinned, therefore disappear.”
But “repent, come into the light, receive grace, and learn obedience.”
Not “your past has permanently named you.”
But “if anyone is in Christ, there is new creation.”
Grace does not give us permission to keep scattering our springs.
Grace gives us a reason to come home.
Maybe your scandal is known by everybody.
Maybe it is known only by you and God.
Maybe your marriage survived.
Maybe it did not.
Maybe you are the betrayed spouse and the word “forgiveness” itself hurts because people have used it to pressure you into pretending betrayal had no consequences.
Biblical forgiveness never requires calling evil harmless.
Reconciliation, trust, and restored access are not identical things, and rebuilding trust after serious betrayal can require truth, repentance, accountability, wisdom, boundaries, and time.
But whether you are the one who betrayed or the one who was betrayed, Jesus Christ remains able to meet you in the ruins.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted His people.
The woman of Samaria carried a complicated relational history.
The woman caught in adultery was dragged publicly into shame.
Again and again, Jesus demonstrated something astonishing:
He could tell the truth about sin without surrendering the sinner to hopelessness.
Grace does not erase truth.
Grace meets us in truth and then refuses to leave the repentant sinner where truth found them.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by changing the definition of sin.
Not by calling darkness light.
He rewrites everything by taking people whose stories appeared ruined and making their wounds places where redemption can testify.
The scar remains evidence that there was once a wound.
But it can also become evidence that the wound did not win.
So hear Proverbs 5 again.
“Should your springs be dispersed outside?”
Perhaps today the question is not simply about adultery.
Perhaps it is asking you:
What sacred thing have you been scattering?
Your attention?
Your affection?
Your eyes?
Your intimacy?
Your integrity?
Your covenant?
Your worship?
Your heart?
And what would happen if today you stopped running?
Not tomorrow.
Not after one final conversation.
Not after one last video.
Not after one last meeting.
Today.
Jesus is not asking you to clean yourself before coming to Him.
Come to Him so He can begin making you clean.
Confess honestly.
Repent sincerely.
Seek wise pastoral or professional help where needed.
Put real boundaries around recurring temptation.
If another person is involved, stop feeding the relationship that is destroying faithfulness.

If you have wounded your spouse, understand that repentance is more than being sorry you were discovered. Repentance produces fruit. It tells the truth. It accepts consequences. It stops demanding instant trust. It seeks accountability. It chooses obedience when nobody is watching.
And if you are single, do not read Proverbs 5 as though holiness begins on your wedding day.
Your sexuality already belongs under Christ’s lordship.
Your body is not worthless because you are unmarried.
Your desires do not make you filthy.
And your singleness does not make pornography, casual sex, secret compromise, or using another human being harmless.
Jesus is worthy of your obedience now.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting.
That matters.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy, but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what we knew clearly yesterday. Come back when compromise starts renaming itself as harmless.

Scripture gives legitimate room for believers to materially support Gospel ministry. Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from Gospel work, and he described believers who financially supported his ministry as partners in “giving and receiving.” But Scripture also guards the heart of Christian generosity: “not reluctantly or under compulsion.” Supporting this ministry is therefore not a payment for God’s favor, not a purchase of salvation, and not something we should call your biblical tithe merely because it is recurring. Salvation cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased. Jesus already paid the price we never could.
But voluntary generosity can become one practical way to participate in spreading Gospel truth.
And there is something else we never want hidden behind a paywall.
The mission is not to sell Jesus.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
The mission is to keep putting biblical truth in front of people who desperately need it—and to invite those who believe in that mission to help carry it.
A share costs nothing, but it can carry Scripture into a home we could never enter ourselves.
The person who needs this article may not follow us.
But they may follow you.
Think about that.
Your share could become the doorway through which somebody finally admits they need help.
Your comment could remind another believer that they are not fighting alone.
Your tag could begin a conversation.
Your testimony could point somebody away from shame and toward Jesus.
And your support could help another Gospel message travel farther than it would have traveled without you.
But after everything written here, do not miss the most important invitation.
Before you follow a page, follow Christ.
Before you share an article, ask whether you are willing to let its truth search you.
Because someday your browser history will not matter.
Your follower count will not matter.
Your reputation will not matter.
Your carefully maintained image will not matter.
What will matter is whether the life you kept hidden from people was surrendered to the Christ who saw it all along.
Proverbs 5:21 says that a person’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD.
That sounds terrifying when you are hiding.
Until you remember who went to the cross.
The God who sees completely is also the God who calls sinners to repentance.
The Christ who knows the whole story is the Christ who shed His blood for sinners.
There is no secret darkness Jesus needs you to explain before He understands it.
He already knows.
The question is whether you will keep running from the One who sees you—or finally run toward Him.
Your springs were never meant to be scattered through streets that cannot love you back.
Your soul was never meant to survive on stolen water.
Come home.
Come into the light.
Bring Jesus the chapter you thought destroyed the entire book.
Because the most unforgettable thing about grace is not that Jesus pretends your scandal never happened.
It is that your scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
